title: Truck-Mounted Crane Manufacturing
one_liner: A concentrated US machinery niche building boom trucks, mobile telescopic cranes and related parts for construction, utility, rental, mining and energy customers.
overview: This industry manufactures truck-mounted cranes and related parts, including boom trucks, mobile telescopic cranes, all-terrain cranes and rough-terrain cranes used for construction, maintenance, industrial lifting, utilities, mining and energy work. The 2022 baseline was still shaped by the post-2020 rebound: 2021 revenue was $1.486 billion and the baseline forecast expected revenue to ease to about $1.4 billion by 2026. Current 2025-2026 conditions are mixed. Public and infrastructure work remains supportive, and the US boom-truck market is forecast to grow from $843.1 million in 2024 to $1.130 billion in 2030 at a 2025-2030 CAGR of 5.2%. However, US construction spending in June 2026 was $2.1665 trillion at a seasonally adjusted annual rate, down 3.2% from June 2025, and steel, tariff and financing costs continue to pressure margins and equipment replacement cycles.

key_stats.market_size: 2026 US industry revenue: about $1.4 billion, based on the 2022 IBIS baseline forecast for truck-mounted crane manufacturing
key_stats.growth: 2021-2026 revenue CAGR: -1.0% in the baseline forecast; 2025-2030 US boom-truck market CAGR: 5.2%
key_stats.boom_truck_submarket: 2024 US boom-truck revenue: $843.1 million; 2030 forecast: $1.130 billion
key_stats.construction_demand: June 2026 US total construction spending: $2.1665 trillion SAAR, down 3.2% from June 2025
key_stats.private_nonresidential_construction: June 2026 private nonresidential construction: $745.3 billion SAAR, up 0.1% from May 2026
key_stats.residential_construction: June 2026 residential construction: $877.1 billion SAAR, down 0.3% from May 2026
key_stats.public_highway_construction: June 2026 highway construction: $150.9 billion SAAR, down 0.1% from May 2026
key_stats.steel_imports: 2025 US total steel imports: 25.241 million net tons, down 12.6% from 2024; 2025 finished steel import share: 18%
key_stats.oil_price_driver: 2025 Brent crude forecast: $67 per barrel; 2026 Brent crude forecast: $51 per barrel in EIA August 2025 STEO

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 estimated US industry revenue: about $1.47 billion, derived from 2021 revenue of $1.486 billion and the baseline 2021-2026 CAGR of -1.0%
baseline_2022.growth: 2022 estimated revenue growth: about -1.0% on the baseline forecast path
baseline_2022.employment: 2021 baseline employment: 1,295 workers; 2021-2027 projected employment CAGR: -0.71%

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers sell new boom trucks, truck cranes, all-terrain and rough-terrain mobile cranes, plus attachments, replacement parts, service and aftermarket support. Revenue is tied to fleet replacement by crane rental firms, construction contractors, utility fleets, municipalities, energy producers, mining customers and equipment wholesalers. Larger OEMs also earn recurring 2025-2026 revenue from parts, technician service, used equipment, financing-adjacent dealer activity and fleet lifecycle support.
cost_structure: Steel, fabricated metal, hydraulics, engines, tires, electronics, truck chassis and outsourced components dominate costs. The baseline put 2021 purchases at 55.6% of revenue, making margins highly sensitive to steel prices, chassis availability, tariffs and supplier lead times. Wages were $170 million in 2021, while 2025-2026 automation, lean manufacturing, telematics and service software are shifting costs from direct labor toward engineering, software, compliance and field-service capability. Tariffs on steel, aluminum and derivative products in 2025-2026 raise input-cost and pricing risk for crane OEMs and importers.
major_players: The Manitowoc Company: US-listed crane OEM with National Crane boom trucks and Grove mobile cranes; 2025 net sales were $2.2 billion, up 2.9% from 2024, and 2025 non-new machine sales were $690 million, up 10% from 2024.

Tadano Ltd. / Manitex: Tadano completed the Manitex acquisition on January 2, 2025, adding Manitex mobile truck cranes, PM knuckle boom cranes, Valla electric cranes and Oil & Steel aerial work platforms.

Link-Belt Cranes: Lexington, Kentucky manufacturer of telescopic and lattice boom cranes, including truck-terrain, rough-terrain and all-terrain models; 2026 CONEXPO lineup included the 120|HT truck crane and 90|RT 2 rough-terrain crane.
Terex Utilities: US producer of utility-oriented truck-mounted aerial devices, digger derricks and related equipment; 2025 TRX Series launch targeted utility distribution and trouble-truck work.
Altec Industries: privately held US maker of boom trucks, cranes, digger derricks and utility equipment serving electric utility, telecom, tree care and contractor fleets.
Elliott Equipment Company: US maker of boom trucks, truck-mounted aerial work platforms and material-handling equipment for construction, utility and municipal fleets.
current_dynamics: In 2026, replacement demand is improving in utility, infrastructure, industrial maintenance and rental channels, but the cycle is not broad-based. June 2026 total construction spending was below June 2025, residential work remained pressured by interest rates, and nonresidential work was only slightly positive month to month. Manufacturers are leaning into higher-capacity models, telematics, safety systems, aftermarket service and domestic production claims to offset cyclical new-equipment demand. Steel and aluminum tariffs, lower 2025 steel imports, and commodity-price volatility keep pricing and working-capital discipline central to profitability.
whats_growing: Infrastructure, utility grid work, data-center-related electrical construction, public highway work, fleet safety upgrades, emissions-compliant engines, telematics, load-monitoring systems and aftermarket service are growing. US boom-truck revenue was $843.1 million in 2024 and is forecast to grow at a 2025-2030 CAGR of 5.2%. Manitowoc reported 2025 non-new machine sales of $690 million, up 10% from 2024, showing the shift toward parts, service and lifecycle revenue.
whats_shrinking: Residential construction-driven crane demand is weaker in 2026, with June 2026 residential construction at $877.1 billion SAAR and down 0.3% from May 2026. Oilfield-related demand faces a softer 2026 outlook because EIA forecast Brent crude at $51 per barrel in 2026 after $67 per barrel in 2025. Import availability is tighter in steel-heavy supply chains, with 2025 total US steel imports down 12.6% from 2024 and finished imports down 17.1% from 2024.
recent_developments: 2025-01-02: Tadano completed its acquisition of Manitex, adding mobile truck cranes and aerial work platforms to its global lifting portfolio.
2025-06-03: The White House announced Section 232 steel and aluminum tariffs rising to 50% effective June 4, 2025, increasing cost risk for metal-intensive crane manufacturing.
2025-08-12: EIA forecast Brent crude at $67 per barrel in 2025 and $51 per barrel in 2026, signaling softer oilfield equipment demand into 2026.
2025-10-07: Terex launched the TRX Series telescopic aerial devices for utility distribution and trouble-truck applications.
2026-02-19: AISI reported 2025 US total steel imports of 25.241 million net tons, down 12.6% from 2024, and a 2025 finished import market share of 18%.
2026-08-03: Census reported June 2026 US construction spending of $2.1665 trillion SAAR, down 3.2% from June 2025.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is modestly positive for demand quality but not for all volumes. Infrastructure, utility, industrial maintenance and fleet replacement should support orders, while residential construction weakness, high financing costs, tariff pass-through and softer oil-price expectations limit upside. Industry revenue is best viewed near the baseline 2026 level of about $1.4 billion, with growth opportunities concentrated in boom trucks, utility bodies, safer higher-capacity models, telematics and aftermarket service rather than broad new-unit expansion.
one_sentence: Truck-mounted crane manufacturing remains a small, mature US industry where infrastructure and utility demand are improving, but high steel exposure, tariff uncertainty, weak residential construction and softer oil-price expectations keep 2026 growth uneven.

title: Tugboat & Shipping Navigational Services in the US
one_liner: A mature, port-linked marine services industry that moves with vessel calls, trade volumes, fuel costs and harbor safety rules.
overview: The industry provides the harbor infrastructure services that let ships enter, berth, shift and leave US ports safely. Tugboat services are the largest revenue stream, followed by pilotage, navigational support, towing, salvage and other marine services. The market is fragmented, with many local operators serving specific ports and waterways, while larger fleets compete in dense trade corridors, petroleum terminals and major container gateways. Current demand is mixed but resilient: 2025 US trade value expanded, major container gateways remained near record volumes, and 2026 import demand has been volatile because shippers pulled cargo forward ahead of tariff and fuel-cost changes. Lower expected 2026 diesel and crude prices help operating costs, but also reduce fuel-surcharge revenue.

key_stats.market_size: 2026 estimated industry revenue of about $5.1 billion, based on the 2022 IBISWorld baseline and its 2022-2028 projected CAGR of 0.95%.
key_stats.growth: 2026 estimated revenue growth of about 1.0%; 2022-2028 projected CAGR was 0.95%.
key_stats.profit_margin: 2022 profit margin was 14.1% of revenue; 2027 baseline projection was 14.8%.
key_stats.employment: 2022 employment was 17,059 workers; 2027 baseline projection was 18,808 workers.
key_stats.establishments: 2022 establishments were 1,159; 2027 baseline projection was about 1,101 enterprises and continued location growth.
key_stats.trade_indicator: 2025 US goods and services exports were $3.432 trillion, up 6.2% from 2024, and imports were $4.334 trillion, up 4.8%.
key_stats.port_indicator: 2025 Port of Los Angeles vessel arrivals were 1,898, up from 1,807 in 2024, while container volume was 10.2 million TEUs versus 10.3 million TEUs in 2024.

baseline_2022.growth: 6.5% revenue growth in 2022 after 6.8% growth in 2021 and a 5.7% decline in 2020.
baseline_2022.profit: $686 million in 2022 profit, equal to a 14.1% margin.
baseline_2022.wages: $1.532 billion in 2022 wages, about 31.5% of revenue.
baseline_2022.service_mix: 2022 revenue mix: tugboat services 62.9%, navigational and transportation-related services 18.1%, towing services 6.0%, all other services 13.0%.

how_it_makes_money: Operators charge vessel owners, ocean carriers, terminal operators, energy shippers, government agencies and insurers for harbor assist, docking and undocking, pilotage support, escort towing, barge and ship movements, marine salvage, wreck removal, emergency response and related vessel services. Pricing is usually per job, per vessel movement, under port contracts or under longer-term customer agreements, often with fuel surcharges and premiums for specialized safety, salvage or high-horsepower work.

cost_structure.labor: Labor is the largest structural cost: 2022 wages were $1.532 billion, about 31.5% of revenue, reflecting licensed pilots, captains, engineers, deck crews and dispatch operations.
cost_structure.fuel_and_purchases: Fuel, lubricants, vessel parts and outside services are the second major cost bucket; diesel volatility affects both direct expense and fuel-surcharge revenue.
cost_structure.capital_and_depreciation: Fleet ownership, maintenance, dry-docking, insurance and financing are material because modern harbor tugs are expensive and must meet safety and emissions requirements.
cost_structure.profit: 2022 profit was 14.1% of revenue; margins benefit from high utilization and fuel pass-throughs but compress when vessel calls fall or crews and boats sit idle.
cost_structure.compliance: 2025-2026 costs are rising for operators exposed to California harbor craft emissions rules, Tier 4 repowers, shore-power or charging infrastructure, and alternative-fuel pilot projects.

current_dynamics: Trade volumes and vessel calls are supporting demand, but the pattern is uneven. 2025 US trade value rose, Los Angeles stayed near record container levels, New York-New Jersey handled 8.9 million TEUs in 2025, and 2026 imports saw tariff-driven front-loading. That creates strong short bursts of harbor-assist demand followed by softer periods. Fuel is moving from a revenue tailwind to a margin variable: EIA's 2025 STEO expected Brent to average $67 in 2025 and $51 in 2026, reducing diesel pressure but also lowering surcharge revenue. Emissions compliance is now a real fleet-planning issue, especially in California, where tug and harbor craft operators face cleaner-engine and zero-emission pressure.
whats_growing: Ship-assist demand at high-volume container gateways and energy terminals in 2025-2026.
Larger, higher-bollard-pull harbor tugs serving megaships; Los Angeles logged 146 megaship calls in 2025 versus 122 in 2024.
Electric, hybrid and Tier 4 tug investment, including Crowley's 2024 eWolf and California compliance-driven fleet planning into 2026.
Pilotage, escort and safety-sensitive services at congested or restricted waterways.
Emergency response, salvage and disaster-related marine support where storms, groundings or oil-risk events require specialized crews.
whats_shrinking: Fuel-surcharge revenue when diesel and crude prices ease; EIA's 2026 Brent forecast was $51 per barrel versus $67 in 2025.
Small operators' room for error as labor, insurance, dry-docking and emissions compliance costs rise.
Export-linked harbor work in ports where loaded export TEUs lag imports; Los Angeles loaded export TEUs fell 4.3% in 2025 versus 2024.
Predictable seasonal planning, because 2025-2026 tariff front-loading shifted cargo into earlier peaks and softer later periods.
Older uncontrolled and Tier 1/Tier 2 diesel harbor craft in regulated markets.
recent_developments: 2024-06: Crowley christened eWolf, the first fully electric ship-assist harbor tugboat in the US, at the Port of San Diego.
2025: US goods and services exports rose 6.2% to $3.432 trillion and imports rose 4.8% to $4.334 trillion, supporting port-service demand.
2025: Port of Los Angeles handled 10.2 million TEUs, slightly below 2024's 10.3 million TEUs, but vessel arrivals rose to 1,898 from 1,807.
2025: Port of New York and New Jersey handled 8.897 million TEUs, up 2.3% from 2024.
2025-08: EIA forecast Brent crude at $67 per barrel in 2025 and $51 in 2026, pointing to lower marine fuel pressure.
2026-07: NRF/Hackett expected major US container ports to reach a record 2.47 million import TEUs in July 2026 as importers front-loaded cargo ahead of tariff changes.
outlook: The 2026-2028 outlook is low-growth but operationally important. Baseline demand should rise with waterborne trade, port calls and large-vessel handling needs, keeping industry revenue near $5.1 billion in 2026 and growing roughly 1% annually absent a trade shock. Margin upside comes from higher utilization, lower diesel costs and fleet efficiency; downside comes from tariff-driven cargo volatility, high mariner wages, interest costs, insurance, dry-docking and emissions-related capital spending. Consolidation is likely to continue in major ports where scale, dispatch reliability and compliant fleets matter most.
one_sentence: US tugboat and shipping navigational services operators earn fees for ship-assist towage, pilotage, docking, escort, salvage and related harbor services, with demand tied to vessel traffic at commercial ports and margins shaped by labor, fuel and fleet renewal costs.

title: Tunnel Construction
one_liner: Specialized U.S. tunnel builders construct, repair and maintain rail, highway, water, sewer and utility tunnels, with demand driven mainly by public infrastructure budgets and a small number of megaprojects.
overview: Tunnel Construction covers new tunnel work, reconstruction, rehabilitation and maintenance for transportation and utility assets, excluding ordinary road and highway construction. The industry is mature, capital-intensive and highly dependent on federal, state and local buyers; the baseline IBISWorld report showed 2021 revenue of $5.1 billion and 9,884 employees, while the April 2025 IBISWorld update estimated a smaller 2025 market of $2.1 billion, 559 businesses and 5,651 employees after several years of project timing volatility. Demand is concentrated in complex public works: rail and subway tunnels, highway crossings, sewer conveyance, water supply tunnels and outfall systems. The business is fragmented, with no company holding a large enough 2024 market share for IBISWorld to identify as a major market-share leader, but large packages are often won by joint ventures of heavy civil specialists.

key_stats.businesses: 559 businesses in 2025, down at a 0.5% CAGR from 2020 to 2025
key_stats.public_construction_context: U.S. public construction spending was $541.2 billion SAAR in May 2026, up 0.5% from April 2026
key_stats.transportation_construction_context: U.S. total transportation construction spending was $6.121 billion NSA in May 2026; public transportation construction spending was $4.448 billion NSA in May 2026
key_stats.water_sewer_context: U.S. water supply construction spending was $35.670 billion SAAR in May 2026; sewage and waste disposal construction spending was $53.235 billion SAAR in May 2026

baseline_2022.market_size: About $5.0 billion in 2022 revenue, inferred from the baseline 2021 IBISWorld revenue of $5.106 billion and its 2021-2026 decline outlook
baseline_2022.growth: About -2.4% in 2022 on the baseline 2021-2026 forecast path
baseline_2022.baseline_source: The provided November 30, 2021 IBISWorld baseline reported 2021 revenue of $5.106 billion, 2021 profit of $260 million, a 2021 profit margin of 5.1%, 706 establishments, 699 enterprises, 9,884 employees and $696 million in wages.

how_it_makes_money: Contractors earn revenue by bidding fixed-price, design-build, construction-manager/general-contractor and subcontract packages for new tunnels, shafts, cross passages, lining, ground treatment, mechanical systems, waterproofing, rehabilitation and routine maintenance. Public agencies provide the dominant funding: the 2021 baseline attributed more than 55.0% of revenue to state and local projects and 37.1% to federally funded projects, while private toll-road, rail and utility work accounted for 5.2%.

cost_structure.labor: Wages were $696 million in 2021, equal to about 13.6% of 2021 revenue; labor demand is specialized and union-heavy on many urban megaprojects.
cost_structure.materials_and_subcontracts: Concrete, steel, precast segments, grout, membranes, pumps, electrical systems, TBMs, muck handling, trucking, cranes and specialty subcontractors are major cost lines; IBISWorld identified purchases as the largest 2025 operating cost component.
cost_structure.equipment_and_capital: Capital intensity is medium to high because tunneling requires TBMs, shafts, ventilation, dewatering, ground monitoring and marine or urban staging equipment.
cost_structure.profit: The 2021 baseline profit margin was 5.1%; 2025 profitability remains exposed to inflation, interest rates, change orders, geotechnical surprises and tariff-related equipment costs.
cost_structure.risk_costs: Schedule delay, differing site conditions, safety compliance, environmental mitigation and insurance/bonding can materially change margins on a small number of large contracts.

major_players: Hampton Roads Connector Partners JV: Dragados USA, Flatiron Constructors, VINCI Construction and Dodin Campenon Bernard
Tutor Perini and other regional heavy civil contractors
current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 market is being pulled in two directions. Aggregate construction spending softened in 2026, with total U.S. construction spending down 1.5% year over year in May 2026, but tunnel-specific backlog is supported by unusually large rail, subway and water projects. The Hudson Tunnel Project alone has a $16.0 billion program cost, a $6.88 billion FTA Capital Investment Grant signed in July 2024 and up to $4.1 billion in RRIF loans closed in FY2024. In 2026, FTA announced $20.6 billion in FY2026 transit funding, including $14.6 billion in IIJA formula funding, and New York officials announced 2026 CIG allocations of $700 million for Gateway Hudson Tunnel and $307 million for Second Avenue Subway Phase 2. At the same time, high interest rates, public budget scrutiny, permitting, labor availability and geotechnical risk continue to limit broad-based growth outside megaproject corridors.
whats_growing: Rail and transit tunneling is growing because signed federal grant agreements have moved Gateway Hudson Tunnel and Second Avenue Subway Phase 2 from long-delayed plans into funded work programs. Water and wastewater tunneling is also supported by aging assets, resiliency needs and population growth; May 2026 water supply construction spending was $35.670 billion SAAR and sewage/waste disposal spending was $53.235 billion SAAR. Rehabilitation demand is expanding as many U.S. tunnels exceed 50 years of age and agencies prioritize reliability, flood protection, ventilation, waterproofing and state-of-good-repair work.
whats_shrinking: Small discretionary tunnel work and private-funded tunnel development remain constrained by high financing costs, long permitting timelines and the availability of bridge, elevated highway and surface alignment alternatives. The 2025 IBISWorld update shows the overall industry was still smaller than the 2021 baseline, with 2025 revenue of $2.1 billion versus 2021 baseline revenue of $5.1 billion, and businesses down to 559 in 2025. New construction outside a few federally backed megaprojects remains uneven, while maintenance-only work is steadier but lower-ticket.
recent_developments: July 2024: FTA signed a $6.88 billion Full Funding Grant Agreement for the $16.0 billion Hudson Tunnel Project, and the Build America Bureau executed up to $4.1 billion in RRIF loans.
August 2024: Gateway Development Commission awarded a $466 million Palisades Tunnel package to Schiavone Dragados Lane JV, with work expected to run through 2027.
May 2025: NYC DEP said the final connection for the Delaware Aqueduct Bypass Tunnel would require a new procurement and was not expected to be completed until after 2027.
May 2026: Traylor/Walsh/Skanska JV was awarded the $1.29 billion Hudson River Tunnel section contract for Gateway Package 1C.
May 2026: Senator Gillibrand announced FY2026 CIG funding allocations of $700 million for Gateway Hudson Tunnel and $307 million for Second Avenue Subway Phase 2.

June 2026: Los Angeles County's Clearwater Project reported continued repair and re-entry progress after the tunnel breach, with the broader approximately $700 million wastewater tunnel program still targeting 2027 completion subject to change.
outlook: The 2025-2030 outlook is modestly positive but uneven. IBISWorld’s April 2025 update says the market is projected to grow over the next five years from a 2025 base of $2.1 billion, helped by federal transportation funding and the Gateway Tunnel grant. Growth is likely to be lumpy rather than linear because annual revenue depends on when a few multibillion-dollar packages reach notice-to-proceed, tunnel boring and fit-out phases. The strongest demand pools through 2030 are Northeast rail capacity, New York subway expansion, Virginia highway capacity, California wastewater resilience and municipal water tunnel rehabilitation. Main downside risks are federal funding politics after FY2026, cost inflation, tariffs on specialized equipment, environmental delays and contractor margin erosion from geotechnical events.
themes: Transit capacity and Northeast Corridor resilience
High capital intensity and specialized labor
Fragmented contractor market with JV delivery
one_sentence: The U.S. Tunnel Construction industry is a volatile, project-driven heavy civil niche that fell to an estimated $2.1 billion in 2025 revenue after a 2020-2025 CAGR of -1.8%, but 2024-2026 federal commitments to rail, transit and water tunnels have improved the near-term backlog outlook.

title: Turbocharger Manufacturing
one_liner: U.S. turbocharger manufacturing is a small, concentrated auto-supplier niche supported by fuel-efficiency rules and hybrid vehicles but capped by battery-electric adoption and tariff-sensitive supply chains.
overview: Turbocharger manufacturers make exhaust-driven compressors used mainly in gasoline and diesel engines for passenger vehicles, light trucks, commercial vehicles, and some industrial applications. The industry benefits when automakers downsize engines, add hybrids, and comply with fuel-economy and emissions rules. It is challenged by battery-electric vehicles, which do not use conventional engine turbochargers, and by cross-border auto-parts trade exposure. The 2022 IBISWorld baseline placed U.S. industry revenue at $1.786 billion; using the baseline outlook and 2025 vehicle-market recovery, 2025 U.S. industry revenue is estimated at about $1.85 billion.

key_stats.growth: 2025 estimated U.S. revenue growth: +1.8%; 2026 outlook: -1.0% to +1.0%
key_stats.profitability: 2022 baseline EBIT margin: 5.0%; 2025 supplier margins improved at large global players, with Garrett Motion reporting 2025 adjusted EBIT margin of 14.2% and BorgWarner reporting 2025 adjusted operating margin of 10.7% across continuing operations
key_stats.demand_base: 2025 U.S. new-vehicle sales: 16.3 million units, up 1.8% from 2024
key_stats.production_base: 2025 U.S. motor-vehicle assemblies: 10.18 million units at a seasonally adjusted annual rate average
key_stats.technology_penetration: Model year 2024 gasoline turbocharged engines: more than 44% of U.S. vehicle production; model year 2025 preliminary gasoline turbo share: 44.8%
key_stats.trade_exposure: 2022 baseline imports: $943.5 million, equal to 39.2% of U.S. domestic demand; 2022 baseline exports: $319.8 million, equal to 17.9% of revenue

baseline_2022.product_mix: 2022 gasoline turbochargers: 52.3% of revenue; 2022 diesel turbochargers: 47.7% of revenue; 2022 rebuilt gas turbochargers: 8.9% of revenue

how_it_makes_money: The industry sells original-equipment turbocharger systems and related components to engine manufacturers, vehicle OEMs, and auto-parts manufacturers, with aftermarket and remanufactured units providing a smaller but steadier revenue stream. Revenue depends on vehicle production schedules, turbo fit rates, diesel and commercial-vehicle demand, OEM platform awards, export orders, and pass-through of steel, aluminum, alloy, logistics, and tariff costs.
cost_structure: 2025 cost pressure is concentrated in machined castings, grey iron, aluminum, stainless steel, nickel-iron-chromium alloys, precision bearings, actuators, electronics, skilled manufacturing labor, engineering, tooling, warranties, freight, and tariffs. 2022 baseline profit margin was 5.0%, showing limited room for small manufacturers to absorb volatile materials and labor costs. Garrett reported 2025 cost of goods sold of $2.853 billion on 2025 net sales of $3.584 billion, illustrating the high materials and manufacturing-content profile of turbo suppliers.
current_dynamics: In 2025, the market was helped by U.S. new-vehicle sales of 16.3 million units and by EPA data showing gasoline turbo penetration around the mid-40% range in model year 2024-2025 vehicles. Hybrid vehicles are supportive because many still use downsized combustion engines with turbochargers. Battery-electric vehicles remain the structural headwind because they remove the internal-combustion engine and conventional turbocharger from the powertrain. 2025-2026 tariffs on automobiles, auto parts, steel, and aluminum add complexity for a highly global supply chain, especially for components moving across North America, Europe, and Asia.
whats_growing: 2025-2026 growth is strongest in turbochargers for hybrid powertrains, variable-turbine-geometry systems, e-boosters, e-turbos, electric compressors, fuel-cell air compressors, commercial-vehicle applications, power-generation and data-center-adjacent turbine systems, and remanufactured aftermarket units. Garrett reported nearly 50 million global turbocharger units produced in 2025 and continued hybrid awards, while BorgWarner reported a 2025 North American hybrid VTG turbocharger award expected to begin production in 2028.
whats_shrinking: Conventional turbo demand tied to pure internal-combustion light vehicles is shrinking in the long term as battery-electric vehicles gain share. Diesel light-vehicle applications remain structurally weaker than gasoline and commercial diesel applications. 2026 light-vehicle production expectations are softer, with Garrett assuming 2026 light-vehicle industry production down 1% to 3% from 2025 and S&P Global Mobility projecting 2026 U.S. auto sales of 15.8 million units, down more than 3% from 2025.
recent_developments: 2025-04: U.S. Proclamation 10908 imposed a 25% tariff on imported automobiles and certain automobile parts, with parts effective no later than 2025-05-03 and USMCA-related exceptions for qualifying parts.
2026-01: Cox Automotive/Kelley Blue Book estimated 2025 U.S. new-vehicle sales at 16.3 million units, up 1.8% from 2024 and the best result since 2019.
2026-02: EPA’s 2025 Automotive Trends Report reported model year 2024 gasoline turbocharged engines at more than 44% of U.S. vehicle production and model year 2025 preliminary turbo share at 44.8%.
2026-02: Garrett Motion reported 2025 net sales of $3.584 billion, up 3.1% from 2024, and said global turbocharger production rose to nearly 50 million units in 2025.

2026-02: BorgWarner reported 2025 net sales of $14.316 billion and 2025 Turbos & Thermal Technologies sales of $5.772 billion; light-vehicle turbochargers represented about 21% of 2025 company net sales.
2026-05: S&P Global Mobility projected 2026 U.S. auto sales of 15.8 million units, down more than 3% from 2025, signaling a softer 2026 production environment for suppliers.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is flat to slightly down for conventional U.S. turbocharger manufacturing because vehicle production is expected to soften and BEV adoption continues to reduce addressable engine content. The medium-term offset is that hybrids, range-extender architectures, commercial vehicles, fuel-economy compliance, and industrial air-compression uses still need advanced boosting technology. By 2027-2028, growth is more likely to come from awarded hybrid turbo programs, e-turbos, e-compressors, and aftermarket installed-base service than from simple growth in combustion-vehicle volumes.
themes: Concentrated supplier base with OEM platform awards
Tariffs and metals costs pressure margins
E-turbos and electric compressors reshape product portfolios

one_sentence: In 2025, the industry remained tied to recovering U.S. vehicle sales and high turbo penetration in gasoline engines, while 2026 demand is expected to be flatter as light-vehicle production softens and suppliers pivot toward hybrid, e-turbo, and industrial air-compression applications.

title: Tutoring & Driving Schools in the US
one_liner: A fragmented consumer education market where learning-loss tutoring and digital test prep are growing faster than mature in-person driving instruction.
overview: The industry covers exam preparation, academic tutoring, automobile driving schools and miscellaneous non-degree instructional services, excluding colleges, universities, trade schools, fine arts, athletic instruction and language schools. IBISWorld's 2022 baseline put 2021 revenue at $14.2 billion and projected 2026 revenue of $15.4 billion, implying slow real growth after the pandemic rebound. The post-2022 market has split: K-12 tutoring demand remains elevated because schools are still addressing achievement gaps, while consumer test-prep demand is being reshaped by test-optional admissions and the fully digital SAT. Driving schools remain a steady, regulated local service tied to teen licensing and safety, but they are less scalable than online tutoring.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 estimated industry revenue of about $15.1 billion; 2026 projected revenue of about $15.4 billion based on the 2022 IBISWorld 2021-2026 CAGR projection in 2021 dollars.
key_stats.growth: 2021-2026 projected CAGR of 1.8% from the 2022 IBISWorld baseline; 2025-2026 demand indicators are mixed, with private exam-prep and tutoring payroll employment at 105,900 in July 2026 versus 97,100 in July 2025 according to BLS.

how_it_makes_money: Revenue comes from hourly or package-based tutoring, recurring online tutoring memberships, standardized-test preparation courses, school and district tutoring contracts, driver education classroom fees, behind-the-wheel lesson packages, permit/license preparation and niche personal instruction courses. Larger tutoring operators add subscription models, institutional contracts, franchise fees, curriculum licensing and digital platform access fees.

cost_structure.labor: Instructor, tutor, support and management wages are the largest expense; the 2021 baseline wage bill was $5.527 billion, about 39.1% of revenue.
cost_structure.rent_and_facilities: Physical tutoring centers and driving schools carry rent, utilities, insurance and vehicle-related facility costs, while online tutoring lowers location costs but raises platform and support spending.
cost_structure.marketing: Customer acquisition is material because households can switch among local tutors, franchises, online marketplaces and free resources.
cost_structure.technology: Online tutoring and digital test prep require learning platforms, scheduling, video, assessment content, AI tools, cybersecurity and product development.
cost_structure.vehicles_and_insurance: Driving schools incur fleet acquisition or lease costs, fuel, maintenance, insurance and compliance expenses.
cost_structure.profit: The 2021 baseline profit margin was 8.1%; margins are constrained by tutor pay, online competition, school procurement cycles and high fixed costs for in-person formats.

current_dynamics: Demand is strongest where services solve measurable learning gaps or mandated licensing requirements. In June 2025, national data cited by Stanford's National Student Support Accelerator indicated that 42% of public school principals reported high-impact tutoring, with prevalence between 37% and 46% over the prior three years. The SAT became fully digital in the US in March 2024, and the class of 2024 had more than 1.97 million SAT takers, supporting new digital-prep products even as test-optional admissions reduce mandatory prep demand. BLS payroll data show private exam-prep and tutoring employment at 105,900 in July 2026, up from 97,100 in July 2025 but down from 108,900 in June 2026, suggesting seasonality and uneven institutional timing. Driving schools remain supported by graduated licensing and safety needs; the CDC's 2026 teen-driver guidance notes that teen crash risk remains highest among ages 16-19.
whats_growing: High-dosage and high-impact K-12 tutoring sold to districts and schools in 2025-2026.
Online tutoring memberships and hybrid tutoring models that combine human tutors, diagnostics and AI-enabled practice.
Digital SAT and adaptive-test preparation after the US digital SAT launch in March 2024.
Early-grade reading and math remediation, especially where districts continue post-pandemic intervention programs.
Flexible, local driver education tied to state licensing, parent demand and teen safety concerns.
whats_shrinking: Paper-based SAT prep and legacy classroom-only test-prep formats after the SAT's 2024 digital transition.
Purely discretionary enrichment that depends on household budgets when consumer confidence weakens.
Federal stimulus-funded tutoring contracts as pandemic-era education relief funding rolls off and state/district procurement becomes slower.
Undifferentiated local tutoring with no digital delivery, measurable outcomes or school-channel access.
High-overhead in-center formats in markets where online tutors and marketplace pricing compress fees.
recent_developments: 2024-03: College Board launched the first fully digital SAT weekend administration in the US and completed the SAT Suite's digital transition.
2024-09: College Board reported more than 1.97 million class-of-2024 SAT takers, up from 1.91 million in the class of 2023, with 68% testing during SAT School Day.
2025-06: National data cited by Stanford's National Student Support Accelerator showed 42% of public school principals reported offering high-impact tutoring.
2025-10: Harvard CEPR and Accelerate released a High-Dosage Tutoring Data Toolkit for states, districts and vendors to monitor implementation.
2026-02: Graham Holdings reported 2025 Kaplan supplemental education revenue of $317.2 million, up 9% from 2024.
2026-02: Nerdy reported Q4 2025 revenue of $49.1 million, up 2% year over year, while noting federal and state funding delays affecting high-dosage tutoring contract timing.
outlook: The industry should grow slowly in aggregate through 2026, with upside concentrated in institutional K-12 tutoring, digital tutoring platforms, AI-assisted diagnostics and premium test-prep niches. The baseline 2026 revenue projection of $15.4 billion remains a reasonable anchor, but the mix is shifting away from traditional in-center consumer tutoring toward online subscriptions and school-funded interventions. Margin performance will depend on tutor utilization, platform efficiency, insurance and vehicle costs for driving schools, and whether state and district tutoring budgets replace the temporary federal stimulus surge.
one_sentence: Tutoring and driving schools sell supplemental academic help, exam preparation, driver education and other non-degree instruction to households, schools and institutions, with 2025-2026 demand supported by high-dosage tutoring adoption, digital SAT participation and steady teen-driver safety needs but pressured by online price competition and funding delays.
